newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Poor response to S.Africa govt severance package.
newsitem.headline: Poor response to S.Africa govt severance package.

text.p: The South African government's voluntary severance package was not attracting as many as people as hoped, which could mean the Cabinet will be forced to make a final decision on staff cuts, officials said on Friday.

Addressing a public service and administration sub-committee, they said that if the voluntary severance package did not work, retrenchments might become an option once again despite their unpopularity.

Chief director of human resource planning Girlie Majola-Pikole told the sub-committee that although her department had set a target of cutting 100,000 jobs for each of the next three years, so far only 3,512 voluntary severance applications had been approved this financial year with another 15,048 pending.
The 100,000 a year was an "anticipated figure but Cabinet might still have to take a decision on the real numbers" as departments did not seem to be keen to make the decision themselves.
"It does not look like the package is delivering the kind of numbers that we thought," Majola-Pikoloe said.
It had been decided to move away from retrenchments to voluntary severance packages because "forced retrenchments as a tool had negative labour relations impacts.
"At this stage, the effort is to try and build a strong, co-operative relationship and partnership between government and the unions," she said.
Voluntary severance packages were also two to three times cheaper for government than retrenchments, and it had been decided to freeze retrenchments.
But this did not mean government "will not at any stage review its decision about utilising the retrenchment package route to effect rightsizing."
The freeze had been in place for three months so far and government would review its decision from time to time to measure progress.
Some committee members expressed concern about publicity that some civil servants were receiving severance packages worth more than one million rand.

Chief director of remuneration Flip Vos said the reports were sometimes misleading as the large payments usually consisted mainly of pension payments with benefits making up a relatively small amount.
